catalog_locator: printed p. 1135 (PDF p. 7 of the SEAlang offprint), section 3.4 'Noun formatives', parenthetical remark
catalog_quote: In Sengseng, the usual noun formative is a suffix -Nin. The resemblance to -Na is suggestive, but cognacy is uncertain, not so much because of the final consonant (these forms in Mengen often take a further possessive suffix -na) but because of the vowel. (POC *a usually remains a in Sengseng except under the influence of i or u in an adjacent stressed syllable.) Tolai seems to lack a cognate suffix.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Not in the listed works, but the reader's conflicts note repeats the 2026-09-17 check's claim that the five open Chowning papers are 'equally silent on Sengseng stress'. Spot-check of those files in the seng1281 folder: Chowning 1978, 'Comparative grammars of five New Britain languages', PL C-61, printed p. 1135 (PDF p. 7 of, in the noun-formative discussion: '(POc *a usually remains a in Sengseng except under the influence of i or u in an adjacent stressed syllable.)' This asserts that Sengseng has word stress (umlaut is conditioned by a stressed syllable) but gives no position, so no rule is recoverable (would classify as unclear or contradictory / no position stated, not none found). sources.note: Catalog checks only: OLAC lists a single description-type item (Throop & Throop 1980 SIL survey, not online); no Organised Phonology Data, no PARADISEC deposit, no published Sengseng dictionary. The earlier scan's 'Chowning & Goodenough 2016 A dictionary of the Sengseng language' does not exist at ANU; the 2016 A-PL volume is the Lakalai (Nakanai) dictionary, whose preface (p.14) says Chowning 'compiled draft dictionaries' of Sengseng and Kove (unpublished).

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1985. Rapid lexical change and aberrant Melanesian languages: Sengseng and its neighbours. In A. Pawley & L. Carrington (eds), Austronesian linguistics at the 15th Pacific Science Congress, 169-198. Pacific Linguistics C-88. DOI 10.15144/PL-C88.169
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Phonological remarks (pp.174-179; n.12 p.192) cover the three voiced stops written p t k, /t/ often trilled, v~w allophony, initial consonant clusters, author's admitted failure to phonemicise the vowels ('arbitrarily reproduced forms as if there were only five vowels'), reduction of CVCV roots to monosyllables, dropping of a first vowel identical to the second (kalat ~ klat) and a-umlaut before i/u. No mention of stress or accent.
